newsitem.title: USA: U.S. civil rights commission criticizes Florida city.
newsitem.headline: U.S. civil rights commission criticizes Florida city.

text.p: A U.S. civil rights investigator Thursday criticised police in St. Petersburg, saying rogue officers could spark more race riots like the two that rocked the Florida city last fall.

"There is a clique within the police department with a significant pattern of misconduct. I advise special training because these people represent the spark that could bring about more disturbances," Bobby Doctor, southeastern regional director for the U.S. Civil Rights Commission, said as the commission released results of its investigation of the riots.

On Oct. 24, 1996, the shooting death of a black motorist by a white police officer set off a night of rioting in the city's predominantly black south side. No one was killed or seriously injured but there was millions of dollars in property damage.
Another riot followed a month later with gunfire directed at police and firefighters when a grand jury ruled that the October shooting was justifiable homicide by the officer, James Knight.
Knight said he shot through the windscreen of a car driven by Tyron Lewis, 18, whom he had pulled over for speeding, after Lewis bumped him with the vehicle.

Doctor also criticised business, financial and white religious institutions for failing to step to the forefront in solving racial problems in St. Petersburg. He compared St. Petersburg's police department unfavourably to that of Tampa, just across Tampa Bay, saying Tampa's police department had a "zero tolerance" policy about race discrimination and fired violators.
He said St. Petersburg adopted a "zero tolerance" policy on paper but he had seen no evidence that it had taken effect.
St. Petersburg Mayor David Fischer said the department was working on improving police-community relations.

"We have rewritten the policies. It is a zero tolerance policy. We are giving more sensitivity training to those officers," he said. He said the department had identified 20 to 25 officers as needing more sensitivity training.
